point: The chapter reviews prior work to expose gaps and opportunities for the thesis.
The chapter is organised by EV charging, batteries, demand response and flexibility markets, ending with a summary against the research questions.
Some sections come from the authors' earlier project thesis and were revised.
Rapid EV growth in Norway strains the grid, yet smart charging can serve as a flexible demand response resource.
EV charging can shift load and cut losses and costs, but degradation, hardware needs and social barriers obstruct this.
High EV penetration causes low voltage in a Taiwanese grid, and smart charging is proposed to mitigate it.
Concentrated EV loads cause voltage and frequency problems, so smart charging is vital, though optimising for distribution can harm transmission.
In Trondheim apartment buildings, private chargers stay plugged in longer, giving more flexibility, and EVs are the main flexible load.
EVs can give DSOs flexibility for voltage control and congestion relief, at the price of coordination, new markets and a new DSO role.
Shifting charging to off-peak hours cuts user costs and, for the grid, clips peaks and reduces losses.
Batteries give fast flexibility that improves stability and cuts costs, but their economics depend on market and tariff structures.
A Finnish energy community coordinating a battery and EVs can profit from the frequency restoration reserve market.
Campus battery and V2G participation in the Norwegian fast reserve market cuts costs slightly, but missing investment analysis makes savings uncertain.
A battery can mitigate rebound effects after demand response events, though the evidence is weak due to a single-day analysis.
Coordinated battery operation in an energy community improves distribution voltage, and degradation-friendly operation postpones replacement.
Battery sizing for an apartment building depends on the demand response type, tariff design and investment costs.
Demand response means users alter consumption in reaction to price signals or operator requests, putting the end user in focus.
Price-based demand response shifts usage with prices and tariffs, and the section covers time-of-use pricing and demand charges.
A home battery under time-of-use pricing in a South African household cut costs and peaks.
Exposing flexible resources to energy prices and demand charges cuts cost, with flexible EV charging mattering most.
A V2G parking lot earns most under one time-of-use tariff, though that tariff limits participation in incentive-based programmes.
Incentive-based demand response depends on adequate notice time and remuneration, both relevant to this thesis.
An EV parking lot cut costs in an incentive programme, but the study ignored how much notice the signal gave.
Only a 12-hour notice time made an incentive programme viable for an EV parking lot, since flexibility shrinks afterwards.
Voltage control by consumers costs them money, so remuneration is needed, which makes it an example of incentive-based demand response.
Belgian DSOs buying flexibility from PV households save more in grid expansion than they pay in remuneration.
The section presents real flexibility programmes and markets to give context for how demand response signals affect cost.
Tibber's Grid Rewards pays private EV owners for smart charging but is limited to that group and handles demand charge inconsistently.
Euroflex is a large Norwegian demonstration project paying varied small and large participants for flexibility.
Norwegian DSO incentive programmes lack a standard design, as each leaves out a key parameter such as duration or notice time.
Most reviewed studies use flexible batteries or EVs for profit or savings, and their insights apply to energy communities.

The following paragraphs summarise takeaways per research question and point to motivating gaps.
Battery design, tariffs and remuneration all shape the flexibility and economics of demand response.
Price-based and incentive-based demand response with EVs and batteries can relieve grid strain and save costs for users.
The literature on load shifting largely overlooks rebound effects, which is the gap this thesis addresses.
The section reviews rolling horizon, receding horizon and SDDP applications to choose the thesis methodology.
Longer planning horizons in rolling horizon give better solutions but cost more computation, and a 24-hour scope misses long-term effects.
For a Malta microgrid, an 11-hour planning horizon matched deterministic results under rolling horizon.
Rolling horizon cuts household costs but cannot capture monthly peaks alone, requiring other methods for long-term consequences.
Receding horizon with a scenario tree lets a commercial building battery cut costs, but few scenarios and imperfect price revelation limit it.
Receding horizon control of a radiator exploits building thermal mass to deliver sizeable demand response potential.
SDDP can coordinate storage and generation for households under uncertainty while avoiding dimensionality problems, but lacked updated forecasts.
SDDP medium-term hydropower cuts improve a short-term model, with a trade-off between time resolution and computation.
SDDP handles hydropower environmental constraints, although non-convexity arises and relaxation was needed.
Combining SDDP with rolling horizon cuts computation and gives more realistic hydro-thermal scheduling, though strict constraints risk infeasibility.
SDDP future-cost curves with a combined rolling-receding framework cut peaks for an EV lot, yet one state variable suggests other methods.
A short dynamically updated horizon combined with SDDP gives both short-term adaptability and long-term consequences, so it suits this thesis.
